stances.claim: Velasco's last-day promulgation of the PDO rule -- filling the gap left by the abolition of DOJ hold departure orders -- exemplifies his career ethic of assiduously working till the final moment.

Over 1,000 full-length ponencias with zero backlog is an exceptional record, and Justice Jose C. Reyes Jr. is 'a known exemplar of the constitutional ideal of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.'
MMDA v. Manila Bay (Dec. 18, 2008) -- Velasco's most far-reaching decision per Carpio -- established 'continuing mandamus' as a judicial tool for environmental enforcement.

Velasco's political-undertone votes (Marcos burial, Mindanao martial law, Sereno ouster) drew mixed reactions -- validating that 'justices cannot please everyone' and 'every litigation has at least two sides.'
stances.rhetorical_move: balanced acknowledgment of controversy without personal judgment

stances.claim: Retirement at a healthy 70 is not farewell but 'changing tires to prepare for a new journey' -- and Marinduque can expect more service from him.

notable_anecdotes: Velasco still fighting on the morning of his retirement (August 7) to get the PDO rule promulgated -- with active help from JJ Perlas-Bernabe and Gesmundo -- as a parting gift to the Court.
Acting CJ Carpio singling out MMDA v. Manila Bay as 'probably the most far-reaching' of Velasco's 1,000+ ponencias during the retirement speech.

The PDO rule: RTCs (not the DOJ) may issue precautionary departure orders on ex-parte application by prosecutors showing probable cause for crimes punishable by imprisonment of at least 6 years and 1 day.

Hacienda Luisita v. PARC (July 5, 2011) -- ending 'eons of row' over 4,915 hectares, declaring the 30-year stock distribution plan disadvantageous to 6,296 farmer-beneficiaries, and ordering physical land distribution.

Velasco's family tableau: wife Lorna was a congresswoman and is now the mayor of Torrijos; son Lord Allan Jay is the incumbent Marinduque congressman; daughter Tricia Nicole is a party-list representative.

one_paragraph_summary: In a valedictory tribute to Justice Presbitero J. Velasco Jr., Panganiban opens with the vignette of Velasco still at his desk on the morning of August 7, 2018 -- his retirement day -- fighting to get the Supreme Court to promulgate his Precautionary Departure Order (PDO) rule, filling the gap left by Genuino v. De Lima (April 17, 2018, per J. Reyes Jr.), which had abolished the DOJ's legally unsupported hold-departure and watch-list orders. With help from JJ Perlas-Bernabe and Gesmundo, Velasco succeeded: RTCs may now issue PDOs ex parte upon prosecutor's showing of probable cause for crimes punishable by at least six years and one day of imprisonment. Over a 12-year tenure, Velasco wrote more than 1,000 full-length ponencias plus thousands of minute resolutions, leaving zero backlog for successor Justice Jose C. Reyes Jr. -- described as 'a known exemplar of the constitutional ideal of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.' Acting CJ Carpio, in his retirement speech, singled out MMDA v. Concerned Citizens of Manila Bay (December 18, 2008) as probably the most far-reaching -- a unanimous ruling upholding the constitutional right to a balanced ecology and directing government agencies to continuously clean the 1,800-km² bay, introducing the novel 'continuing mandamus' concept (which later spawned the April 10, 2010 Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases). Hacienda Luisita v. PARC (July 5, 2011) ended 'eons of row' over 4,915 hectares, declaring the 30-year stock distribution plan disadvantageous to 6,296 farmer-beneficiaries and ordering physical land distribution. His political-undertone votes (Marcos burial, Mindanao martial law, Sereno ouster) drew mixed reactions, consistent with the truism that justices cannot please everyone. Velasco paid tribute to his supportive family -- wife Lorna (former congresswoman, now Torrijos mayor), son Lord Allan Jay (Marinduque congressman), daughter Tricia Nicole (party-list rep.) -- and said that retiring at a healthy 70 really means 'changing tires to prepare for a new journey,' a sentiment the author endorses with a forecast of more service from the patriarch of Marinduque.
